beats.t: The three sat around the ember jar in the underground kitchen. Nobody spoke first. Only two of them could have made a sound even if they tried.
I shouldn't have left you alone. I'm sorry.
Not the cat's fault. It's the pig's fault for doing exactly what they were told not to.
(He's right, so why is it so annoying?)
Yeoni opened their mouth wide, then closed it. Not even escaping air made a sound. Their throat felt like an empty box.
The crow took more than your voice. The entire path through which words emerge. The path of Hurting Officer.
Then the noon concert's finished. The one meant to make the first sound can't talk.
(You're supposed to make the first sound!)
Yeoni pointed a hoof at Moka. He shook his head. Yeoni pointed again. He shook it harder.
Stop pointing. I'm not doing it.
Yeoni, try writing.
Moka took a small blackboard from the wall. With chalk in their mouth, Yeoni wrote: Moka, you do it.
The instant the final stroke ended, the letters faded gray and scattered like dust. Nothing remained on the board.
(Writing doesn't work either?)
Wow. That crow is thorough. Like a tax collector.
Writing carries words too. The crow blocked that path as well.
So this pig can't do anything now?
(Anything?)
Yeoni pulled the board back. This time, instead of letters, they drew a circle with short lines around it. A sun.
The picture did not fade. White chalk remained on the board.
Drawing still works.
A skewer below the sun. A smiling face beside the skewer. ...Free skewers again?
(Correct.)
The force poured out through words is called Hurting Officer; the force made through your hands, Eating God. The crow stopped words. The power to make things remains.
(Then I've still got half left!)
Yeoni added more pictures. The market. A grill. People in a line. Stamps on their hands fading little by little.
You want to grill skewers at the market? Without talking?
Yeoni nodded vigorously. Then drew an otter beside the pig in the picture. A slightly better-looking otter than the real one.
...Why'd you make me handsome?
Flattery.
(Not flattery. Your future appearance.)
Fine. Let's do it. One condition. I only grill. I'm not standing in front of customers.
The voiceless pig will face the customers. Fair enough.
(A perfect team.)
In the middle of the gray market, Moka dragged over an abandoned cart and set a grill on it. Yeoni placed the blackboard at the front. Sun, skewer, smiling face.
Nobody approached. People glanced at the board and passed. On this island, free food meant a trap.
See? Nobody's coming.
Yeoni took a skewer into the middle of the street and acted out eating it. Very dramatically.
(Mmm. That's the taste. That's it.)
One bite, eyes closed. Two bites, hooves cradling cheeks. Three bites, lying on the ground and flailing.
What is that supposed to be?
A review. A five-star one.
A passing child stopped. One stamp on their hand. A child whose laughter had been taken. They looked down at the flailing pig.
The corners of the child's mouth twitched. Laughter tried to emerge, caught on the stamp. Yeoni held out the skewer.
The child took a bite. A corner of the gray stamp faded like singed paper. The child smiled. Silently, but unmistakably.
...It's real. The stamp burned away.
People who had seen it approached the cart one by one. First three. Then ten. A line formed.
Not enough skewers! Cat, make some dough!
Look at the shape of my paws.
Never heard of being so busy you'd borrow a cat's paws?
Not just a cat.
Just or not, knead it a hundred times.
A cat in a hat's pride is being mixed into dough.
(Pride-filled dough ought to be chewy.)
Eventually Yeongnyangi pulled the bowl close. Flour dusted his hat brim and white fur. Watching children's shoulders shook.
Yeoni handed out skewers along the line. Gestures instead of words. Hot, so blow. Tasty, give a thumbs-up. Finished sticks go here.
(Everyone understands without words!)
Customers, one blow each, please. You're spitting on the grill.
Tap, tap-tap came from the market's far side. Captain Drum put his box beside the cart and began keeping time. Heads nodded to his rhythm.
One corner of the gray market regained a little color. Smoke from the skewers rose golden.
Then metal rang above the market roofs. Everyone in line froze. A wing's shadow covered the cart.
Unlicensed business. Unauthorized fine dining. Unauthorized rhythm.
And silent incitement.
How is it incitement when nobody even spoke!
(I really didn't! Not one syllable!)
Laughter is the beginning of song.
People backed away. Yeoni took a skewer and walked toward the crow. Their hoof shook, but the skewer stayed level.
(Have one too.)
The defendant may not speak.
Yeoni nodded, then held out the skewer again.
The crow's wing knocked it away. It rolled onto the ground. Yeoni did not pick it up. Instead, they brought over the blackboard.
Yeoni, step back.
Yeoni drew. A stage. A small person onstage. Laughing people below. They erased the laughing faces and drew them again. This time, applauding faces.
(I wish it had been like this. That day.)
The crow looked at the drawing. Its mask shook. Crack. A split opened down the middle.
Through it appeared a face. A boy. The shadow of someone about fifteen or sixteen, frozen with a microphone in hand.
...A person?
Don't look.
The crow covered its cracked mask with a wing. Its voice split low, the same crack heard in the courtroom.
Don't look. Don't laugh. Nobody.
The crow took flight. A few feathers fell. One landed on Yeoni's blackboard, covering the drawn stage.
The market people stayed beside the cart. Nobody fled. Someone picked up the fallen skewer, dusted it off, and placed it on the cart.
The old woman. One of her three stamps had faded. She gave Yeoni a thumbs-up.
(I got five stars.)
Don't cry. If you cry, I'll... no, I won't cry.
Today's business was a success. Without a single word.
Night. The three lay on a roof overlooking the Sundial Stage. Above the island's highest stage hung the stopped sun.
One side of it had been eaten black. The shadow, only fingernail-sized when they arrived, now covered half the sun.
Bigger than yesterday.
The more fire we light in the market, the more they hurry over there.
(What if it covers everything?)
If Byeong is devoured, this island will be trapped in night. Noon will never return.
(Then my skewer stall becomes a permanent night market.)
Your face shows exactly what you're thinking. Business, isn't it.
Then when? The noon concert.
When the next bell rings. The moment the sundial casts its final shadow.
Yeoni touched their throat. Empty. A pig unable to make the first sound had promised a noon concert.
(What if I really can't do anything?)
Don't make that face.
Moka pressed a paw onto Yeoni's head. An awkward touch.
You made a hundred people smile at the market today without saying a word. That's harder than being a good talker.
(...Moka complimented me.)
(Wish I could record this. Oh, right. No voice.)
Not a compliment. A statement of fact.
Yeoni began nodding off. Moka draped his apron over them. Then he noticed Yeongnyangi's forepaw.
Cat. What's with that paw?
Nothing.
Charred skin showed through white fur. 傷—wound. The character was clearer than yesterday.
You got hurt in court. By the pig's fire.
Don't tell. Not this child.
Why? They need to know to be careful.
If Yeoni knows, they won't make a sound at noon. For fear of hurting me.
Moka stared at Yeongnyangi for a long time. Then pulled the apron up to cover the sleeping pig's ears.
...Tell them after noon. Or I will.
An otter threatening a cat.
Cooks are good at threats. Have to be, to last in front of a fire.
On the high dais of the empty courtroom, the crow crouched without removing its cracked mask. Threads of sol and mi glittered inside its robes.
That pig knows nothing about singing. So why?
The crow traced the crack with a wingtip. Wind slipped through. It smelled like the wind that had struck its face onstage long ago.
Then the shadow below the dais stretched long. Five black fingers bloomed at its end.
You are wavering, child.
You have swallowed the pig's voice. Now it is time to swallow noon.
When the sun is fully devoured, I will gather all your feathers too. And every song that remains.
